title: Fraud & Compliance
description: Build fraud detection with rule engines and ML scoring, minimize PCI DSS scope with tokenization, implement audit logging, and handle chargebacks at scale.

segments.text: Global payment fraud exceeds forty billion dollars annually. A fraud detection system must evaluate every transaction in under one hundred milliseconds — block too slowly and the fraudster wins, block too aggressively and legitimate customers leave. Stripe reports that their ML models catch ninety-five percent of fraud while maintaining a false positive rate under one percent.

The first layer is a rule engine. Velocity checks: more than five transactions in ten minutes from the same card? Flag it. Amount thresholds: transaction over ten thousand dollars from a new account? Review it. Geographic impossibility: transaction in New York, then London, twenty minutes apart? Block it. Rules are fast and interpretable but rigid.

ML models score each transaction with a fraud probability. Features include: device fingerprint, transaction amount relative to user history, time of day, merchant category, shipping-billing address mismatch, and real-time velocity. The model produces a score from zero to one. Above zero point eight: auto-block. Between zero point five and zero point eight: manual review. Below: approve.

Real-time feature computation is critical. You need the user's transaction count in the last hour, their average transaction amount in the last thirty days, and the merchant's chargeback rate — all computed in sub-millisecond. Use Redis for real-time counters and a precomputed feature store for historical aggregates. Stale features mean missed fraud.

Your fraud model blocks a legitimate high-value customer who's buying an expensive gift while traveling abroad. They call customer support angry and threaten to leave. How do you balance fraud prevention with customer experience?
segments.thought_prompt: How do you reduce false positives for high-value customers without increasing fraud exposure?

segments.text: PCI DSS compliance governs how you handle card data. The key strategy: minimize scope. Never store raw card numbers. Use a tokenization service — the card number goes in, an opaque token comes out. Only the tokenization service handles raw card data. Everything else uses tokens. This reduces your PCI scope from your entire infrastructure to one isolated service.

Every payment action must be audit logged: who performed what action, on which resource, at what time, from which IP address. Audit logs are immutable — stored in append-only systems with cryptographic chaining so tampered entries are detectable. Regulators can request audit trails during examinations. Missing logs mean fines.

Chargebacks are when a customer disputes a charge with their bank. The merchant must respond with evidence within seven to ten days. At scale, you need automated chargeback handling: detect the notification, pull transaction evidence, generate a response package, and submit it. High chargeback rates — above one percent — can get you banned from payment networks.

Fraud models degrade over time as fraudsters adapt. Monitor model performance daily — track precision, recall, and the fraud-to-legitimate ratio. Retrain monthly with fresh data. A/B test new models in shadow mode before deployment. PayPal retrains their fraud models weekly and has seen fraud patterns shift completely within three months of a model launch.

Design a fraud detection system for a payment platform processing five million transactions per day. It must evaluate each transaction in under fifty milliseconds with less than half a percent false positive rate.
segments.thought_prompt: Design fraud detection for 5M daily transactions: sub-50ms latency, <0.5% false positive rate.

segments.text: Fraud and compliance require layered defense: rule engines for known patterns, ML models for emerging threats, tokenization for PCI scope reduction, immutable audit logs for regulatory compliance, and automated chargeback handling. The Staff-level principle: in payments, the cost of being wrong is measured in real money — every architectural decision must prioritize correctness and auditability.
